articles.title: Why Bangladesh descended into violence ahead of Hasina’s planned return
articles.summary: Supporters of ousted PM, who lives in self-imposed exile in India, have protested against rejection of her return.
articles.body:
Bangladesh has deployed paramilitary troops to help contain a wave of violence that erupted after supporters of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina staged protests against the government’s rejection of the ousted leader’s planned return to the country.

At least four people have been killed and police stations, banks and even the ancestral home of the former interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner, Muhammad Yunus, have been attacked in a week of violence.

Violence erupted after supporters of Hasina’s now-banned Awami League party took to the streets as part of weeklong protests that overlapped with the anniversary of the former leader’s death sentence last year. Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia for crimes against humanity related to the 2024 student-led protests.

Earlier this month, Hasina requested a new passport and identity card to allow her to return to Bangladesh. She has been living in self-imposed exile in India after fleeing the country in the wake of the July 2024 student-led uprising.

But the Bangladesh government, led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, says she is a convicted criminal, and she can only return under the extradition treaty with India.

Rahman has blamed India for the unrest. “It is not only that; they have not looked at the interests of Bangladesh and its people. At the same time, the country across the border, where they have fled to, is their master… To satisfy those masters, they have again started conspiring against Bangladesh and its people,” Rahman said in parliament on Friday.

So why does Hasina still want to return to the country, and are the recent protests spontaneous or orchestrated?

What do we know about the deadly protests?

Since mid-November, arson attacks and violence have been reported across 28 districts of Bangladesh.

At least four people have been killed in the political violence since November 14, including three political activists and a bus worker who died when his vehicle was torched, according to local media reports.

Two men from the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) were killed in the Narail district, according to the AFP news agency. In retaliation, BNP supporters set ablaze more than a dozen homes belonging to Awami League supporters in the district.

A Narail resident, who asked not to be identified for fear of reprisals, said as many as 50 houses had been damaged in the district.

“We are terrified by the clashes,” he told AFP. “We have asked our women and children to stay inside unless it is absolutely necessary.”

Late Wednesday, police said the ancestral home of Yunus was set on fire in the port city of Chittagong. It was not immediately clear who was behind the blaze.

“Criminals set fire to the eastern side of the house. The area was being used as a storeroom,” Chittagong Metropolitan Police spokesman Aminur Rashid said, adding there were no casualties.

Yunus, who was targeted by Hasina during her term in power, has faced hostility from her supporters. Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, said 22 of its branches were subject to arson attacks.

State news agency BSS reported that 90 additional platoons of the paramilitary Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) had been deployed nationwide.

National police chief Md Ali Hossain Fakir told BSS that security had been restored in Gopalganj, Hasina’s hometown and a longstanding stronghold of her party.

“I urge the peace-loving people of this area to stand against those involved in sabotage and disorder,” he added.

Khandakar Tahmid Rejwan, lecturer of global studies and governance at the Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB) and contributing analyst at the United States defence think tank Jamestown Foundation, told Al Jazeera that the protests do not appear to be entirely spontaneous in nature.

“If they were genuinely organic and spontaneous, one would arguably expect to see broader public mobilisation and participation across different parts of the country. Instead, what we are witnessing is a concentration of protest activity in areas such as Gopalganj, Faridpur, and Madaripur, which have traditionally served as strongholds of the Awami League’s support base,” he said.

He noted that while sporadic protests and demonstrations have also been reported in other parts of the country, their scale and geographical spread, at least so far, suggest localised unrest rather than a nationwide mobilisation.

“Although these incidents are concerning from the perspective of public order and political stability, the available pattern of mobilisation does not, at this stage, indicate a level of nationwide momentum that could fundamentally challenge the incumbent government’s position,” he added.

The recent protests began soon after the government rejected Hasina’s request for her passport and identity card on November 9. Hasina served as prime minister from 1996 to 2001, and again from 2009 to 2024, but her nearly 15 years of iron-fist rule have been slammed by human rights organisations.

She was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over her deadly crackdown on the student-led protests in 2024. As many as 1,400 people may have been killed in the violence, according to United Nations estimates.

Hasina has, however, denied these charges and told the Reuters news agency on November 9 that she intended to return to Bangladesh and surrender before a court. Her aides added the date would be announced once various formalities were completed.

But her request has been denied by the current government.

“Bangladesh does not give passports to terrorists who kill thousands of people and flee. It will work under the current extradition arrangements with India to pursue and get the terrorist Hasina handed over,” State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said earlier this month.

The Bangladeshi prosecutor Md Aminul Islam, who secured the death sentence for Hasina at the Dhaka-based International Crimes Tribunal, said she will be executed if she returns home.

“Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” Islam told reporters.

Protesters have also been calling for the ban on Hasina’s party to be lifted and detained leaders and supporters of the party to be released from prison.

Why does Hasina want to return to Bangladesh?

Hasina still enjoys support among a section of the population, while many others want to see her hanged.

Her return could also worsen political tensions as Prime Minister Rahman’s government tries to restore ‌‌stability two years on from the 2024 uprising.

But her game plan behind why she wants to return is unclear.

Some analysts have questioned whether Hasina genuinely intends to return to face the law.

Others have questioned whether she is using the promise to revive her political fortunes from self-imposed exile in India. New Delhi, her close ally for decades, has sheltered her since she fled Dhaka in August 2024. But her continued presence has become a point of contention between the two countries.

Rejwan believes there are several interconnected factors behind Hasina’s renewed emphasis on returning to Bangladesh.

“First, there is the domestic political context. It has been nearly 10 months since the incumbent government assumed power, and during this period, it has faced a number of challenges, including inflationary pressures, economic stagnation and a fuel crisis. While these difficulties are not entirely homegrown and are, to a considerable extent, linked to broader geopolitical and global economic developments, it remains difficult to communicate these complexities to the general public. Their everyday consequences inevitably affect public morale and confidence in the government,” he said.

“Secondly, there is the ongoing political debate surrounding whether the Awami League should remain proscribed or be allowed to resume its political activities,” he added.

He noted that several international actors and civil society voices have advocated lifting the temporary ban and allowing the party to return to mainstream political activities, potentially following the prosecution and sentencing of those responsible for the atrocities committed during the July 2024 uprising.

“Thirdly, there is India’s role, which cannot be entirely overlooked. Sheikh Hasina and several Awami League leaders and activists who fled Bangladesh following the collapse of her government in August 2024 have reportedly continued to receive varying degrees of support from India. There have also been discussions and speculation about whether New Delhi has been exploring possibilities for negotiating her safe return to Bangladesh, potentially under arrangements that would ensure her security, including protection under the custody of the Bangladesh Army,” he added.

Mushfiqul Fazal Ansarey, a senior Bangladeshi diplomat, said that Hasina does not intend to return to face her sentence. “In my assessment, her talk of a comeback is intended to rally supporters and destabilise Bangladesh,” he told Al Jazeera.

The violence, Ansarey said, has extended abroad, with Awami League supporters reportedly attacking Nahid Islam’s entourage in Romford, east London. Islam, who was part of the student-led uprising, is a member of parliament.

“Arson, killings and intimidation cannot be presented as political protest. The neighbouring country should ensure that its territory is not used to organise or incite violence against Bangladesh.”

What are the political ramifications of the Awami League protests?

Besides deploying police forces to contain the protests, in an effort to build unity, Prime Minister Rahman has held talks with Shafiqur Rahman, the leader of the opposition party Jamaat-e-Islami.

The Jamaat’s Secretary-General Mia Golam Porwar told the Bangladeshi newspaper The Daily Star that the two leaders viewed the meeting positively and hoped it would strengthen democracy in the country.

“If this initiative is taken with the intention of moving forward with everyone on board, it will be good. We want to view it positively. If the initiative genuinely has good intentions, we want it to succeed,” he said on Sunday.

Rejwan, from the Independent University of Bangladesh, said that from the Awami League’s perspective, one of the most unfavourable political developments would be the possible convergence of political interests between the BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami, particularly if their existing political differences were set aside in the interest of preventing the Awami League from regaining political ground.

“Beyond the Awami League, Jamaat-e-Islami remains one of the few political organisations in Bangladesh with an established grassroots organisational structure, a relatively disciplined cadre base, and extensive networks of political mobilisation. This gives the party a significant organisational capacity to counter the Awami League’s own entrenched political networks and grassroots mobilisation,” he said.

He highlighted that another crucial variable is the extent of residual popular support for the Awami League.

“If Sheikh Hasina were to return to Bangladesh, how would the politically dormant but ideologically sympathetic sections of the population respond? Would her return reactivate sections of the Awami League’s grassroots support base, or would the party’s political isolation and organisational setbacks limit its ability to mobilise them?” he said.

“Ultimately, the sustainability and effectiveness of any BNP–Jamaat political understanding aimed at containing the Awami League’s political resurgence would depend not merely on elite-level negotiations but also on the ability of both parties to manage their competing political interests and respond to the evolving sentiments of the wider electorate,” he said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges US to release Patriot missiles as Russia kills 7 in Ukraine
articles.summary: Three Russian attacks kill at least six people near Kyiv as overnight Russian shelling kills one in Zaporizhzhia.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged the United States to approve the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles after a week of Russian attacks across 20 regions of the country with the latest ones killing six people near Kyiv and one in Zaporizhzhia.

In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russia launched about 2,700 attack drones, nearly 1,460 guided aerial bombs and 165 missiles over the past week. A significant share of the missiles were ballistic, he said, including some supplied by North Korea.

“Against this backdrop, it is particularly difficult to understand the delays in the delivery of antiballistic systems to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine is short of US-made Patriot interceptors, which can shoot down ballistic missiles.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s partners had already paid for the missiles through a NATO-coordinated programme that funds purchases of US weapons for Kyiv. However, their delivery is still awaiting Washington’s approval.

One of the latest Russian attacks hit a five-storey apartment building early on Sunday in the village of Dymer, north of Kyiv, causing part of it to collapse.

Rescuers later recovered three bodies as emergency crews searched for 10 people, including two children, who were missing, according to Russia’s Interfax news agency, citing Radio Liberty.

Later ⁠on Sunday, two people were ⁠killed when a Russian drone struck a grocery store in the city of Vyshneve, southwest of Kyiv, Governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram, adding that eight ⁠people were injured.

One more person was killed when a strike set a private home ablaze in the city of Bila Tserkva, also in the region of Kyiv, he added.

“The world must stop looking away. Condemn this terror, hold Russia accountable, and act now to stop the killing of innocent Ukrainians,” Tkachenko said on X.

Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the Zaporizhia regional military administration, also said a man was killed overnight in Russian shelling in the city of Zaporizhzhia.

Moscow says it hits cargo ship and power facilities

Also on Sunday, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces struck a cargo ship northeast of Ukraine’s Black Sea port city of Odesa overnight.

The ministry said Russian drones struck the Pravoberezhna electricity facility in Zaporizhzhia, which it said supplied power to Ukrainian arms manufacturers. It reported further strikes on an oil refinery, electrical substations and a data centre operated by MKM Telecom.

In its battlefield update, the ministry claimed Russian forces had taken control of the Ukrainian village of Sosnovyi Bir in the northeastern Kharkiv region and destroyed a launcher for Ukraine’s Neptune coastal missile system.

It also said it struck energy and transport facilities it described as serving Ukraine’s military. The Russian claims could not be independently verified.

articles.title: 'Haven't been invited to discuss Indus': Pakistani minister dodges question on 'cut off hands' threat
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Pakistan's climate change minister Musadik Masood Malik on Sunday dodged a question about his earlier \"cut off hands\" threat over the Indus
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Pakistan's climate change minister Musadik Masood Malik on Sunday dodged a question about his earlier "cut off hands" threat over the Indus Waters Treaty suspension, saying he had not been invited by India to discuss the issue. Malik, who is attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi, also spoke about Islamabad's position on terrorism, saying discussions should be based on evidence.When asked about his earlier warning over the Indus Waters Treaty, Malik said, "When you invite me to discuss the Indus Water Treaty, we will certainly talk about it. You haven't invited me to discuss the Indus Water Treaty at this moment..."Responding to questions on terrorism, Malik said Pakistan was willing to engage in discussions and present evidence."If you are seeking a lasting solution to the issue—rather than merely looking to provoke—then that is how we should proceed...I am offering you a stable, consistent response: whenever discussions take place, they will be based on evidence. I assure you, such discussions will certainly happen...We have stated on many occasions—in various forums—that evidence can be presented bilaterally; we have also suggested that this could be handled multilaterally—you bring your evidence, and we will bring ours..." he said.What was the 'cut off hands' remarkIn October, Malik had warned India over the suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty, saying, "It has already been declared that whoever touches our water, their hands would be cut off."His remarks came after India put the treaty in abeyance following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack. New Delhi has maintained that the suspension will remain until Pakistan stops supporting terrorism.Prime Minister Narendra Modi had earlier said, "terror and talks cannot go together; water and blood cannot flow together."Pakistan, meanwhile, has been facing water shortages in parts of Sindh and Balochistan, with dwindling irrigation supplies affecting agricultural regions. The crisis has also triggered disputes over water distribution within the country.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
articles.summary: The Rapid Support Forces are blamed as drones reportedly hit UN and government buildings, as well as Khartoum’s airport.
articles.body:
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.

The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.

The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan ‘s war increasingly relies on drones.

Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.

Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.

A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.

In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.

The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.

The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.

A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.

Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.

Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.

Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.

The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.

Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.

The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.

The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

articles.title: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.summary: Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the Iran war began, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to re-exert its control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices.
articles.body: Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the Iran war began, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to re-exert its control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices. In October, the number of attacks reported to the Royal Navy-affiliated United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) exceeded 30 for the first time since the US-Iran war began in late February. As of Sunday, at least 22 attacks were reported in November, the second highest figure since the war began, according to a CNN analysis of UKMTO data. The reporting area covers the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Before October, the number of reported attacks in the region averaged around 10 per month. Numbers vary, but data from the International Maritime Organization also points to October as having the highest number of confirmed incidents so far this year. Since the conflict began, the strait has become a heavily contested frontier, with attacks there disrupting oil and gas shipping and sparking global economic fallout. Iran began trying to halt traffic in the wake of the US-Israeli attacks that launched the war. In response, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and as CNN previously reported, Gulf producers have found ways of getting ships through the strait. Commercial traffic through the channel – through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war – remains at a reduced level when compared to the 2025 baseline. As global oil prices fall and the Iran’s domestic crude revenues come under increasing strain, Tehran has been stepping up attacks, with experts saying the country is losing its leverage over the waterway and could escalate attacks further in an attempt to force concessions from Washington. No need for a deal, Trump says The International Energy Agency attributes the recent decline in oil prices to a recovery in Gulf exports. Prices also fell after the US midterm results as concerns over fresh US military action in the Middle East subsided. “Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN. “But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation.” Meanwhile, Iran’s domestic oil revenues are falling sharply as the US blockade of Iranian ports continues to stifle the country’s supply of oil to global markets, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler. “Iranian oil on water outside the (US) blockade zone has hit zero as the last cargoes discharged in China earlier this month. Consequently, Iran’s oil revenues could drop to zero by mid-December,” Kpler reported in late October. US President Donald Trump said this month the US doesn’t “need a deal” with Tehran and ordered Vice President JD Vance to turn his focus elsewhere. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” He later indicated he wouldn’t hesitate to resume military strikes in Iran if necessary. Three tankers struck in Hormuz since Friday During the latest attacks, projectiles struck three tankers exiting the strait on Friday and Saturday, according to Marisks, a maritime risk management company. Marisks did not confirm who was behind the attacks, though it said Iranian involvement was “assessed as likely.” Fire erupted aboard the Captain Leon, a Marshall Islands-flagged chemical and oil tanker, after it was struck at the bow at 3 p.m. UTC (10 a.m. ET) on Friday. All crew were reported safe, Marisks said. The Torkel, a Hong Kong-flagged crude oil tanker, caught fire after being hit in the stern at 5 a.m. UTC on Saturday (midnight ET on Saturday). Less than an hour later, the Arina, also Hong Kong-flagged, was struck in the engine room by a missile. The attacks demonstrate the “continued critical threat” to commercial shipping in the region, Marisks said, particularly through the “southern corridor” near Oman’s coastline which Iran vehemently opposes.

articles.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
articles.body:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.

The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Later, on Sunday evening, the health ministry said it had received injured from another ship that was targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not specifically name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."

If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.

As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.

But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The warship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.

Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."

articles.title: The AI talent war: China is the factory, America the magnet, India an also-ran
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: In the new world order being fashioned by artificial intelligence, scientists such as Fei-Fei Li, Kaiming He, and Anima
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: In the new world order being fashioned by artificial intelligence, scientists such as Fei-Fei Li, Kaiming He, and Anima Anandkumar have become the rock stars of technology, their research breakthroughs, institutional affiliations and career moves followed almost as closely as those of Silicon Valley's billionaire founders. Li is the Stanford AI pioneer who helped usher in the modern deep-learning revolution; He’s ResNet architecture transformed computer vision by making it possible to train much deeper neural networks, and IIT Madras Alum Anandkumar, a Caltech-Nvidia collaborator, is the pioneer of Neural Operators, a new class of AI techniques that can learn and simulate complex physical phenomena. They are among the intellectual heavyweights shaping the technology that will increasingly determine economic and geopolitical power.Their prominence reflects a fundamental shift in the global balance of power: In the contest for AI supremacy, the most valuable resource is no longer oil, gold or even the rare earth minerals needed to manufacture advanced electronics. It is human intelligence -- specifically, the ability to produce, attract and retain scientists of their ilk who are capable of building artificial intelligence. Indeed, as Washington tries to preserve its technological primacy against an increasingly formidable China, India is falling behind on almost every measure, while losing much of the elite AI talent it does manage to produce -- like Anandkumar -- to America.A striking analysis by the Carnegie Endowment, tracking 10,280 researchers whose papers were accepted at NeurIPS 2025, one of the world's premier AI and machine-learning conferences, reveals the extraordinary concentration of talent in China and the US, with India a distant also-ran thanks to its inability to retain its AI elites. Nearly 60% of these leading researchers received their undergraduate education in China, compared with just 13% in the US. But China is also increasingly keeping its talent at home -- 41% of the researchers are now working there. Of the 3,514 leading researchers in the study working in the US, approximately 35.7% were educated in China and 34.5% in America. Together, they account for about 70% of the country's elite AI research workforce.In contrast, India-educated AI researchers numbered just 285, or 8.1% -- figures that should be disappointing for New Delhi, where there is much talk and only modest action on the AI education front. While China educated more than 4,000 researchers in this elite cohort, India accounted for just 411. More strikingly, only about 10% of the Indian-educated researchers stayed back in India; roughly 370, or 90%, went abroad, overwhelmingly to the US.The American talent magnet is however facing political turmoil, with sections of the US national-security establishment becoming increasingly suspicious of Chinese access to advanced American technology, particularly after the recent controversy involving Nvidia. The resulting climate of suspicion has broader implications for Chinese-born researchers, and it played out on Friday with the detention of Eva Yi Xie, a Chinese-born Princeton doctoral student and MIT graduate by immigration authorities at Reagan National Airport, an incident that sent shockwaves through academic circles.Xie, who came to the US as a teenager and has a pending asylum case, was detained while returning from a neuroscience conference. Her lawyers say she had valid work authorization; the Department of Homeland Security disputes her authorization to study. She has not been accused of espionage or any connection to the Nvidia investigation, but her case illustrates how an increasingly restrictive immigration climate can unsettle the very international scientific community on which American technological leadership depends.India’s problems are different; it is not merely a failure to retain talent; it is its inability to produce enough advanced researchers in the first place as revealed by the Carnegie study. China awarded approximately 53,000 science and engineering doctorates in 2022, against 45,000 in the US in 2023. India awarded around 23,000 in 2021. More tellingly, India produced just 621 computer science PhDs, compared with 2,874 in the US. China does not publish a directly comparable standalone figure for computer science PhDs; it classifies computer science doctorates under engineering.But the gap is not simply about numbers. India's share of global citations in computer science AI research rose from approximately 3.2% in 2013 to 6% in 2023. China's stood at about 22.5%. In granted AI patents, China's share reached 70% in 2023, while India's remained negligible, according to a NITI Aayog own assessment.Stanford University's 2025 AI Index offers another telling measure of innovation. US institutions produced 40 notable AI models in 2024, compared with 15 from China. India produced none that met the index's threshold. That does not mean India has no homegrown models: Bengaluru-based Sarvam has emerged as a serious effort, with its more ambitious 30-billion and 105-billion-parameter models arriving in 2026, too late for the 2024 comparison. Meanwhile, the Carnegie study found that India's share of elite AI researchers declined by two percent between 2022 and 2025. Not a single Indian institution featured among the leading universities producing this talent in either cohort. China's Peking University, by contrast, topped the institutional rankings.China's advantage reflects more than two decades of investment in mathematics, science and research institutions, an effort diminished by an NYT report on Saturday that Beijing has been running a secret campaign to help the country’s companies acquire advanced A.I. chips and to gather intelligence on the sector. No such issues with New Delhi so far. Its problem is home-grown – or home "not grown."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Police investigating whether Titans’ Jaylen Harrell assaulted driver before Florida crash
articles.summary: TAMPA, Fla. — Tennessee Titans defensive end Jaylen Harrell was hospitalized in Florida following a serious car crash, and police said Saturday that they were investigating whether he assaulted a ride-share driver.
articles.body: TAMPA, Fla. — Tennessee Titans defensive end Jaylen Harrell was hospitalized in Florida following a serious car crash, and police said Saturday that they were investigating whether he assaulted a ride-share driver. Harrell was in his hometown of Tampa when the crash occurred Friday morning. The Titans said in a statement that he was continuing to receive care in the hospital and they were in constant communication with his family. Tampa police said in a statement that Harrell was a passenger in the back seat of a white Kia Sorento “when he reportedly assaulted the driver while the vehicle was in motion.” The driver, a man in his mid-30s, swerved and struck a second vehicle before colliding with a utility pole. Harrell was thrown forward, struck the windshield and lost consciousness, the statement said. The driver had minor injuries and was treated at the scene, according to police. The driver of the second vehicle, a woman in her early 50s, was not hurt. “The allegations described are unacceptable and have no place in the Lyft community,” a spokesperson for the ride-hailing service said Sunday in a statement. “We have permanently banned the rider’s account from the Lyft platform, reached out to the driver to offer our support, and stand ready to assist law enforcement with an investigation.” The 24-year-old Harrell has not played for the Titans this season. He injured his ACL during the preseason and was placed on season-ending injured reserve. The Titans asked for privacy for Harrell and his family and said they would “provide an update when appropriate.” Tennessee selected Harrell in the seventh round of the 2024 draft out of Michigan. He finished his rookie season with 13 combined tackles and had 25 last season. He had 4 1/2 sacks and a forced fumble in 2025. Harrell’s father, James, also played eight seasons in the NFL. ___ See AP’s full NFL coverage here

articles.title: ‘Disappointing’: Delegates react after COP31 climate talks end without deal
articles.summary: Draft text considered too weak to deal with climate change after oil-producing countries oppose the term ‘fossil fuels’.
articles.body:
United Nations climate talks have failed to secure a deal on how to deal with climate change, prompting UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to express “a very profound frustration”.

Multiple countries and negotiating blocs said on Sunday that the final draft, presented by COP31 presidents Turkiye and Australia, was too weak to fight global warming.

If the text had been approved, it would have acknowledged for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve from the 2015 Paris Agreement.

The talks had extended into overtime after key oil- and gas-producing countries opposed mentions of “ fossil fuels ” in the final text. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for funds to help poorer countries adapt to climate change.

The last time the annual UN climate talks failed to end in an agreement was in Copenhagen in 2009.

Here’s how countries and key parties reacted to the deal’s failure:

“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on ⁠an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of ⁠all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” Guterres said.

The UN chief criticised powerful fossil fuel interests for obstructing climate action, accusing them of distorting scientific evidence, delaying policies and prioritising profits.

The European Union said it will not endorse a deal that “does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate ‌‌change, ‌‌and we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel”.

A spokesman added that the draft deal “does not begin to address the climate emergency that we face”.

Samira Nawa said the EU was willing to accept clauses on adaptation finance but argued that the text did not go far enough.

“This is about the mitigation. It’s about the ⁠⁠fossil fuels not being mentioned. It’s the language on science not being strong enough.”

Kate Hughes said the draft text “moves us backwards on the science” and does not acknowledge the urgency or scale of the climate crisis.

“It should have been instead presenting bold, collective ambition on climate action.”

The Least Developed Countries group said: “We struggled to find meaningful outcomes that respond to the ⁠⁠priorities of the most vulnerable countries like us. … We cannot afford to see backsliding.”

The group is composed of 44 countries that are the most vulnerable to climate change and have contributed relatively little in carbon emissions.

They represent more than 1 billion people and include Pacific island nations, such as Tuvalu and Kiribati, as well as other countries most at risk to the effects of climate change, such as Bangladesh, Nepal and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

“We have been let down on all sides,” the Marshall Islands said. “We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future.”

The delegation for the Pacific island nation said: “This text falls short of what international law requires, what science demands and what our vulnerable communities urgently need.”

It called it “unacceptable” that the text was “silent” on fossil fuels.

Kenya’s delegation complained that the deal did not specifically mention Africa and did not take into account “Africa’s special needs and circumstances”.

“Those who took the lead in emissions cuts take the lead in support.”

The Iraq delegation expressed its “deep concern with some pathways that were taken to divert ⁠⁠from [the] Paris Agreement”.

Sergei Kononuchenko, a Russian delegate, argued that if oil and gas supplies shrink, it would lead to a “switch to dirtier types of fuel and energy poverty, … and the first to suffer would be the poorest”.

“For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel.”

The Saudi delegation said it believed “climate change requires all solutions on the table” and it made no sense for “concrete solutions” to be “taken off the table”.

Murat Kurum, Turkiye’s minister of environment, urbanisation and climate change, said: “We did everything we could. You should not hurt people in the world who really expect something out of this by just being hung up on one word or phrase. … There is no benefit for anyone in a system where you go into negotiations with no result.”

“There will be ‌‌no new text from now on. We will not be carrying out work on a new text in an environment where there is no consensus. We will implement existing decisions.”

Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister of climate change and energy, called the collapse of the talks “very disappointing”.

“A lot of good things happened this COP, a ⁠⁠lot of events which told the clean energy story, a lot of commitments made – like the more than 90 countries that signed the electrification pledge, for example. And all that is good work and a great thing but not enough when it comes to climate action,” he said.

“An obvious issue is the transition away from fossil ⁠⁠fuels, where some parties insisted that must be mentioned. Other parties insisted that if it was mentioned, they would veto.”

articles.title: Russian vessel docked in Libya hit in suspected drone attack, authorities say
articles.summary: Libya’s eastern-based government says a drone attack was likely behind an explosion on a Russian ship docked at a naval base in the coastal city of Benghazi.
articles.body: Libya’s eastern-based government says a drone attack was likely behind an explosion on a Russian ship docked at a naval base in the coastal city of Benghazi. A statement said the vessel had docked for refueling and supplies in the city’s port under a maritime cooperation agreement between the two countries before it intended to return to Russia. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs, taken Sunday, shows a large plume of smoke rising from the city’s port area. Separately, social media video obtained by Reuters shows fire engulfing a ship docked in the port. A joint investigation has been launched with Russia to uncover the circumstances of the incident, and who could have been behind it, according to the eastern-based government. There has been no immediate comment from Russia, and no group or nation has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack. Two military sources in eastern Libya told Reuters that a Maltese-flagged commercial ship was also struck by a boat drone off the Benghazi coast on Sunday, with eastern Libyan naval forces rescuing the crew members. The attacks in Libya come after another Russian ship was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea on Saturday – an attack the Finnish military said was likely carried out by Ukraine. CNN has previously reported on Ukraine’s involvement in operations in Libya, as well as other African nations including Sudan and Mali. One Ukrainian naval drone operator deployed in Libya told CNN earlier this year his unit was using a military base in Misrata, a northwestern city east of Tripoli, as a launchpad to attack Russia’s shadow fleet in exchange for training local forces. Despite the presence of Ukrainian troops in the country, Libya’s eastern government emphasized Sunday that it would not allow its territory to be turned into an “arena for settling scores” or exporting international conflicts. It insisted it was not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war. Since the NATO-backed uprising that toppled long-time dictator Moammar Gadhafi in 2011, Libya has been locked in a bitter political conflict as rival administrations and armed groups vie for power. The oil-rich nation is currently ruled by two governments: the UN-backed Government of National Unity (GNU) in the country’s west, based in Tripoli, and a second administration in the east, called the Government of National Stability (GNS). articles.title: COP31 ends in deadlock: Why countries couldn't agree on fossil fuels
articles.summary: United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday after countries failed to reach a consensus on whether
articles.body: United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday after countries failed to reach a consensus on whether to explicitly mention fossil fuels in the final text. The two-week negotiations, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime, also remained divided over climate finance and other issues. The proposed agreement was rejected by several countries and the European Union because it did not include a reference to fossil fuels.Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, said: “It's unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,”The failure to reach a consensus came despite a larger number of countries being willing to accept the proposal, even reluctantly, on the grounds that an agreement was better than none. Russia and Saudi Arabia had sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document.Why fossil fuels became the sticking pointThe joint Turkish-Australian leadership's final proposal did not mention fossil fuels. This became the central point of disagreement, with several countries and climate groups arguing that any meaningful climate agreement must address the use of coal, oil and natural gas, which drive global warming.Fossil fuels had remained unmentioned in final COP decisions for more than 25 years, according to Alden Meyer of the think tank E3G. That changed three years ago at COP28 in the United Arab Emirates, when countries agreed to “transitioning away from fossil fuels”. The Turkish-Australian proposal reproduced that language, but it failed to satisfy several nations and environmental groups.Another point of contention was the draft's reference to carbon capture and storage, along with a goal for the technology to be used by industrial polluters. Several countries and activists argued that this could weaken efforts to reduce overall emissions.As the proposed agreement fell apart during the plenary session, Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum, who presided over COP31, was absent. Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan announced that the talks had failed to reach a deal.“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that's disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia's Chris Bowen, COP31's president of negotiations.Bowen maintained that the commitment made at COP28 remained in force. “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It's happening. It's happening at speed and it's irreversible.”What else remained unresolvedThe failure to reach an overarching agreement also left several other climate issues unsettled. These included details on transitioning away from fossil fuels, financial support for poorer countries to adapt to climate change, and action on gender and climate. Many of these issues were deferred to next year's negotiations in Ethiopia.Turkey had made global electrification its signature issue at this year's talks. A separate proposal called for countries to increase electricity's share in total final energy consumption from around 21% currently to 35% by 2035.Achieving this would require countries to shift transport, including cars, trucks and planes, from fossil fuels to electricity. It would also involve using electricity instead of coal in industrial production. Nearly 100 countries signed up to the separate pledge.The negotiations over the main agreement also faced criticism over the way the final draft was handled. The proposal was circulated after 3am, leaving negotiators little time to register objections. Several observers and countries blamed the joint Turkish-Australian leadership for the failure.Earlier in the week, Panama's Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro had accused a “petroleum mafia” of holding the talks hostage and called for reforms.The wider climate challengeThe deadlock came at a time when the effects of global warming are intensifying, with increasingly severe heatwaves, floods, storms and droughts. The UN has warned that the world is set to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius warming threshold set under the 2015 Paris Agreement.Earlier this year, the United Nations Environment Programme said crossing the threshold had become inevitable. The focus, UN officials said, should now be on limiting how far temperatures rise beyond it and eventually bringing them down through measures such as removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.Scientists estimate that the world is on track for warming of between 2.7 and 3 degrees Celsius by the end of the century. October 2026 recorded the largest temperature increase above pre-industrial levels of any month, at 1.8 degrees Celsius, according to Berkeley Earth. The organisation also estimated a 97% chance that 2026 would be the warmest year on record.The climate negotiations were further complicated by a global energy shock linked to the war in Iran and a strong El Niño, which amplifies human-caused warming and contributes to extreme weather events.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Ohio father's child-support payment fell from $1,745 a month to about $141 after his children began spending alternate weeks with each parent; a November 19 appeals court upheld the reduction after a second challenge
articles.summary: An Ohio appeals court has upheld a major reduction in a father's monthly child-support payments after his two children began spending alternate weeks with
articles.body: An Ohio appeals court has upheld a major reduction in a father's monthly child-support payments after his two children began spending alternate weeks with each parent. The court on November 19 rejected the mother's second challenge to the revised arrangement, allowing the father to continue paying about $140.71 a month, down from the earlier $1,745.48.The ruling came after the mother, Carrie Connelly, challenged a decision by the Lucas County Court of Common Pleas that modified the couple's shared-parenting arrangement and reduced the father's support obligation. The appeals court found that the trial court had made the required findings to justify the reduction and that its decision was supported by evidence.Why child support was reducedThe couple divorced in 2013 and had a shared-parenting plan for their two children, born in 2007 and 2010. Under the original order, the father, William Connelly, was required to pay the mother $1,745.48 every month in child support.In October 2023, the father asked the court to change the parenting arrangement and make him the children's residential parent. He later amended his request, saying he no longer wanted to end the shared-parenting plan but wanted the schedule modified and his child-support payments reduced.Following a hearing in June 2024, the trial court changed the schedule so that the children would spend alternate weeks with each parent. It calculated a revised support arrangement and ordered the father to pay $140.71 a month, citing the equal division of parenting time.The mother challenged the decision. In October 2025, the appeals court upheld the change in parenting time but sent the child-support issue back to the trial court because it had not made certain findings required to justify the reduction.The trial court issued a fresh order in November 2025, again setting the father's monthly payment at $140.71. The mother then filed a second appeal.Court rejects mother's second challengeThe mother argued that the trial court had improperly relied on information from a separate hearing concerning the allocation of the children's tax exemptions. She also claimed that the reduction was excessive and unsupported by the evidence.The appeals court acknowledged that the trial court had referred to the father's payment of approximately $10,000 for a trip to Spain with the children, information discussed during the tax-related hearing. However, it said any error in considering that information was not serious enough to overturn the ruling.The court noted that the trip was only a small part of the trial court's reasoning. It had also considered that both parents bought clothing and paid other expenses for the children while they were in their respective homes.The trial court had further considered the parents' incomes and their respective shares of the children's expenses. The father was responsible for 55 per cent of those expenses, while the mother was responsible for 45 per cent.Rejecting the mother's argument that the reduction was unreasonable, the appeals court said the trial court had made the necessary findings and its decision was backed by credible evidence.The November 19 judgment affirmed the lower court's order, leaving the father's monthly child-support payment at $140.71You use AI every day. articles.title: Governments fail to reach agreement at COP31 over fossil fuel clash
articles.summary: The United Nations’ COP31 climate talks failed to reach a consensus between international governments amid a clash over fossil fuel regulation. “I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in a Sunday statement. “I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected…
articles.body:
The United Nations’ COP31 climate talks failed to reach a consensus between international governments amid a clash over fossil fuel regulation .

“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in a Sunday statement . “I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands.”

“The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis – and it must do it now,” he stated. “The countries that did least to cause this crisis cannot be left to face its worst consequences alone. This is a matter of climate justice.”

This marks the third time in the climate summit’s three-decade history that international negotiators failed to reach an agreement — first at COP6 in 2000 and second at COP15 in 2009. COP31 ran into overtime for two days following its two-week tenure, but a consensus was still not reached.

The European Union, alongside smaller countries susceptible to climate disasters, reportedly rejected proposals that would have cut certain protections and favored countries that export oil, gas and coal, according to The New York Times . Leading oil-producing countries, such as Saudi Arabia and Russia, also blocked mentions of phasing out fossil fuels at COP31.

Other key issues that created tension in negotiations was the amount of concerted effort by countries to wean themselves from fossil fuels and whether ramping up electricity should only be done with renewables or involve energy sources like natural gas, according to The Associated Press.

Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, energy and the environment, said, while speaking on behalf of the EU, that the final proposal “fails to meet the moment.”

“We will not accept negotiating backward in time and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel,” O’Brien told a room of negotiators . “We will not endorse a covered decision … that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.”

Turkish environment minister Murat Kurum, president of the talks in Antalya, Turkey, stated on social media , “Getting hung up on a single word and stalling the process means dashing the hopes of people expecting good news from us.”

“A system that cannot make decisions benefits no one,” he continued. “If we are talking about sincerity, we must all act accordingly and work together toward our shared goals.”

articles.title: Relive golden age of American road trips at these 10 classic Route 66 stops
articles.summary: Route 66 turns 100 in 2026, and a drive from Chicago to Santa Monica traces the Mother Road's neon signs, vintage diners and small-town main streets.
articles.body: Route 66 has spent a century connecting travelers with the people, places and roadside attractions that help define the American road trip. Stretching about 2,400 miles through eight states from Illinois to California, the historic highway marked its 100th anniversary in 2026, bringing renewed attention to communities along the route. Known as the Mother Road, the highway carried generations of families west during the Dust Bowl and the travel boom following World War II. Today, it gives drivers a chance to revisit a classic era of American life, complete with neon signs, vintage diners and small-town main streets. ROUTE 66 SEES NEON-FUELED RESURGENCE IN TULSA AHEAD OF CENTENNIAL Route 66 author Jim Hinckley previously told Fox News that the road's lasting appeal has always come down to the communities along the way. "From its inception, what it's about is the people. It has always been about the people," Hinckley said. "That's what gives it that infectious magic and enthusiasm." For anyone planning a drive along Route 66, here are 10 stops worth adding to the journey, blending classic landmarks from AARP's online newsletter "The Girlfriend" with small-town gems along the way. 1. Chicago, Illinois The cross-country drive starts in downtown Chicago at the "Begin Historic Route 66" sign across from the Art Institute of Chicago, according to AARP's "The Girlfriend." 5 US DESTINATIONS NAMED TO BEST OF WORLD TRAVEL LIST FOR 2027 BY NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC Before hitting the open road, travelers can grab breakfast at Lou Mitchell's, an old-style diner long known as a traditional first stop for motorists, AARP noted. Visitors can also walk along Jackson Boulevard, which formed part of the original route, or take in views of the city from Skydeck Chicago, according to the outlet. 2. Springfield, Missouri Heading southwest into Missouri brings travelers to Springfield, widely known as the "Birthplace of Route 66." Officials met in the city in 1926 and proposed the name "U.S. Route 66" for the highway linking Chicago to Los Angeles, AARP noted. FOX NEWS' STEVE DOOCY TRAVELS ROUTE 66, UNCOVERS THE STORIES THAT BUILT AMERICA OVER A CENTURY Today, visitors can browse shops along historic Commercial Street, explore the Wonders of Wildlife National Museum & Aquarium or catch a movie at the restored Gillioz Theatre, a 1926 theater that hosted live shows during the route's early years, according to the guide. 3. Oklahoma City, Oklahoma Farther down the road, Oklahoma's capital sits near the middle of the route and showcases Western history and art at the National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum, according to AARP's "The Girlfriend." Travelers can also stroll through the 15-acre Myriad Botanical Gardens or explore the shops and restaurants in the Bricktown Historic District, AARP noted. Those staying overnight can book a room at the Skirvin Hotel, a landmark property that has welcomed guests since 1911, according to the outlet. 4. Vega, Texas Continuing west into the Texas Panhandle, smaller towns show what Route 66 looked like before major interstates took over. In Vega, which was bypassed when Interstate 40 was built, travelers can visit Dot's Mini Museum one block off the old highway, Fox News Digital previously reported. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The free museum stays unlocked so visitors can browse 20th-century antiques, and Dot's granddaughter, Keila Bain, told Fox News her late grandmother inspired a character in the Disney-Pixar movie "Cars." "Our town was bypassed by I-40, but you know, there are a lot of people who travel, who love to go into the town, meet the people, see the places," Bain said. 5. Adrian, Texas Just 15 minutes west of Vega sits Adrian, recognized as the geographical midpoint of Route 66, according to Gary Daggett, president of the Old Route 66 Association of Texas. "It's the nostalgia, ya know. There's so much of American history here at Route 66," Daggett told Fox News Digital. While in town, drivers can stop at the Midpoint Café, which owner Brenda Hammit Bradley said is known for its homemade pies and inspired Flo's V8 Café in "Cars." 6. Albuquerque, New Mexico Crossing into New Mexico, Albuquerque has the longest surviving city stretch of original Route 66, according to AARP's "The Girlfriend." Eighteen miles of neon signs, retro motels and vintage storefronts line Central Avenue, leading visitors from historic Old Town to the art galleries and music venues of Nob Hill, AARP noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Travelers can also ride the Sandia Peak Tramway or spend the night at Hotel Parq Central, a restored building that once served as a railroad hospital, according to the outlet. 7. Painted Desert, Arizona Heading into eastern Arizona, Route 66 passes near the Painted Desert, where old-school roadside attractions still draw passing drivers, Fox News Digital reported. One popular photo stop along that stretch is a large dinosaur model near the highway that dates back to midcentury family road trips. 8. Winslow, Arizona Farther west in Arizona sits Winslow, a desert town immortalized in The Eagles' hit song "Take It Easy," Fox News Digital noted. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ That musical tie has turned Winslow into a lasting stop for music fans and road-trippers looking to visit a piece of American pop culture. 9. Flagstaff, Arizona Flagstaff is one of the best-preserved Route 66 towns and long served as a mountain stop for travelers heading west, according to AARP. Visitors can stop by the Flagstaff Visitor Center and Historic Train Depot to learn how Americans shifted from train travel to road trips in 1926, the outlet said. Travelers can also shop for Native American jewelry or visit the Museum Club, a former log cabin that now hosts country music acts, according to the guide. 10. Santa Monica, California After more than 2,400 miles on the road, travelers reach the Pacific Ocean at the Santa Monica Pier, celebrated as the "End of the Trail" for Route 66. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Visitors can take a photo next to the historic "End of the Trail" sign, ride the pier's solar-powered Ferris wheel or walk along Ocean Avenue to mark the end of the trip, AARP noted. Fox News Digital's Gary Gastelu and Chelsea Torres contributed reporting.

articles.title: Thanksgiving travel forecast: Storms on both coasts could snarl the busiest travel days, including Thanksgiving Day
articles.summary: Storms on both coasts could disrupt Thanksgiving travel, from a soaking Northeast storm Sunday to a possible major storm on Thanksgiving Day.
articles.body:
Millions of Americans hitting the road and skies for Thanksgiving could run into storms on both coasts, starting Sunday and possibly lasting through the holiday itself.

A coastal storm is bringing heavy rain and gusty winds from the mid-Atlantic to New England on Sunday night and into Monday morning. Forecasters are also tracking a potentially strong nor'easter for Thanksgiving Day, and an atmospheric river on the West Coast.

"Each of these storms has the potential to trigger major weather delays at major Northeast and West Coast hubs," the Weather Channel said .

Weather isn't the only problem. Delta Air Lines flights were delayed nationwide Sunday after an outage hit the system the airline uses to calculate planes' weight and balance.

AAA projects that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home between Tuesday, Nov. 24, and Monday, Nov. 30, including 72.9 million by car and 5.96 million on domestic flights.

Nearly half of Delta's flights were delayed as of midday Sunday, according to flight tracker FlightAware, the Associated Press reported . At Atlanta's airport, Delta's main hub, 38% of departures were delayed.

Delta said it was using "manual workarounds" to get flights out while it worked to restore the system. The Federal Aviation Administration briefly halted Delta flights headed to Atlanta at the airline's request, then eased the order to a ground delay. The FAA said on X that the delays "are not related to any FAA air traffic systems."

It's the third major disruption to U.S. air travel in nine days, after the FAA's nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 and a similar outage at United Airlines on Nov. 16. Delta travelers should check their flight status before heading to the airport.

Sunday night and Monday: Heavy rain in the Northeast

A storm that dumped record rain on parts of Florida last week is moving up the East Coast. The National Hurricane Center said Saturday that it was unlikely to become a tropical or subtropical storm, but it is still bringing gusty winds, rough surf and heavy rain.

In New York City, rain could start as early as 2 p.m. Sunday, with the heaviest rain likely between about 5 p.m. and midnight and 1 to 3 inches in total, city emergency officials said . Gusts of 25 to 35 mph are expected, with a few over 40 mph possible Sunday night. Boston could see up to 2 inches of rain and gusts up to 45 mph near the coast. The rain should clear out by Monday afternoon.

"If you're flying, Sunday evening is when the storm is likely to cause the most issues," New York City Emergency Management said, adding that gusty winds Monday could also slow flights.

In Florida, more than 16 inches of rain fell near Cocoa Beach over three days, according to AccuWeather, and the St. Johns River near Cocoa hit 18.6 feet Friday, breaking a record set in 1953. Flooding along the river is expected to linger past Thanksgiving.

Tuesday and Wednesday: Atmospheric river in the West, storms in the Southeast

A strong Pacific storm fed by an atmospheric river is forecast to hit from Northern California to Washington state starting Tuesday. Heavy rain, strong winds and mountain snow could cause significant delays along Interstate 5 between Seattle and San Francisco and on mountain routes including I-80. Airports in Seattle and San Francisco could see delays.

"Drivers along I-5 should prepare for heavy rain that can reduce visibility and leave water collecting on the roadway," AccuWeather meteorologist Haley Taylor said. "Travelers heading into the Sierra will face a different challenge, with heavy snow potentially making mountain routes difficult or impassable."

Southern California is expected to miss the heaviest rain.

In the Southeast, heavy rain and thunderstorms could hit Atlanta and Charlotte on Wednesday, one of the busiest travel days of the year. Delays at those hubs could ripple across the country.

Thanksgiving Day: Possible major storm in the Northeast

Forecasters are increasingly confident that another storm will form off the Southeast coast late Wednesday and move up the East Coast on Thanksgiving, bringing heavy rain and strong winds from the mid-Atlantic to New England.

The National Weather Service in Boston called it a "potentially significant coastal storm" for Thanksgiving into Friday, with gusts along the coast possibly topping 50 mph. Very high tides could also bring coastal flooding, the agency said. Interior parts of the Northeast and the Appalachians could see some snow or ice.

That could be a problem for the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which is set to start at 8:30 a.m. Thursday. The parade's giant balloons can't fly if sustained winds top 23 mph or gusts top 34 mph, Fox Weather reported .

Forecasters say the storm's exact track and timing could still shift.

Another storm could form in the East during the busy return weekend, while more Pacific storms could hit the West Coast. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically one of the busiest travel days of the year.

Forecasters advise travelers to check forecasts for both their departure and arrival cities, and to keep an eye on flight status before heading to the airport.

articles.title: Virginia reports first measles-linked death of 2026 in child younger than 5
articles.summary: The death comes within days of health experts stripping the US of its measles elimination status, amid uptick in cases.
articles.body:
A young child has died in Virginia, marking the first case of a measles-related death in the southern state for the year 2026.

The Virginia Department of Health made the announcement on Friday, just days after the United States lost its designation as having eliminated the highly contagious virus.

State authorities declined to provide details about the child’s death, citing the family’s privacy. It was disclosed, however, that the child was younger than five.

Virginia has reported 220 cases overall this year, most of them in the central part of the state. The vast majority of the cases were among people not vaccinated against the virus.

They include 40 children ranging from infants to age four, and another 75 children aged five to 12, according to state health department data as of November 19.

“Virginia has not had a measles-related death since 1978,” according to Frederic Bertley, an immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry, a research centre in Ohio.

He added that the spread of measles is evidence that the virus is gaining a foothold and becoming a growing problem for the US.

Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported its eighth measles-related ⁠⁠death of the year last week and confirmed 1,631 measles cases, as of November ⁠⁠20.

Wisconsin also reported two deaths in 2026, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death of 2026 in early November.

In that case, the victim was reportedly a seven-month-old child. It was the state’s first measles-related death in more than three decades.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does ‌‌not specify the states where the deaths were recorded.

It has also tracked more than 5,800 cases nationally in 2026, the most of any year since 1991.

In August, President Donald Trump issued an executive order reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccinations, falsely suggesting that the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine could be dangerous.

“You have the MMR; we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together, there could be a possibility they are quite lethal,” Trump said.

The CDC has said it remains committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said.

The CDC has provided approximately $100m in additional funding to state and local health departments since August to strengthen vaccination efforts, surveillance and outbreak response.

articles.title: Man convicted of starting California's deadly Palisades Fire in 2025 that destroyed over 6,800 buildings
articles.summary: A 30-year-old man has been found guilty of starting the devastating Palisades Fire in California, which killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800
articles.body: A 30-year-old man has been found guilty of starting the devastating Palisades Fire in California, which killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings in January 2025.A federal jury in Los Angeles convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht of two arson-related charges on Friday, holding him responsible for a fire that initially broke out on January 1, 2025, and later reignited six days afterwards, turning into one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.According to the BBC, the blaze swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu, destroying entire neighbourhoods. Rinderknecht faces between five and 20 years in prison on each count. He is scheduled to be sentenced on March 17, 2027.The verdict came nearly five months after his first trial ended in a mistrial, with jurors unable to reach a unanimous decision. The first jury had reportedly deadlocked 10-2 in favour of acquittal.Rinderknecht had pleaded not guilty to the charges. His lawyer, Steve Haney, said the defence was disappointed with the verdict but respected the jury's decision. He indicated that the legal team would review its options regarding a possible appeal.How the fire started and what prosecutors arguedProsecutors said Rinderknecht started a brush fire on January 1, 2025, which continued burning undetected beneath the ground in root systems before reigniting on January 7 and developing into the catastrophic Palisades Fire.During the retrial, prosecutors presented cellphone location data, photographs, security camera footage and witness testimony to establish that Rinderknecht was near the area where the initial fire started.They also presented evidence about his behaviour in the hours before the blaze, including testimony from passengers who travelled with him and messages he exchanged with his girlfriend. Prosecutors said he had been angry and frustrated that night.Investigators also argued that the January 7 wildfire was a continuation of the original fire and ruled out other possible ignition sources, including fireworks.After the initial fire broke out, Rinderknecht reportedly called 911 more than a dozen times. Prosecutors also told the court that he searched ChatGPT on his phone, asking: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?" They argued that these actions were an attempt to create an alibi.The defence, however, challenged the prosecution's account of where the fire originated. Haney argued that investigators could not conclusively establish that Rinderknecht was responsible and suggested that fireworks could have started the blaze.Deadly California wildfires killed 31 peopleThe Palisades Fire was among several major wildfires that swept through the Los Angeles region in January 2025. The fires collectively killed 31 people and destroyed around 16,000 structures.US federal prosecutor Bill Essayli said the guilty verdict brought some measure of justice to families who lost loved ones and thousands of residents whose lives were affected.Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the verdict could not bring back those who died or erase the suffering of affected families.She added that many residents were still struggling to rebuild their homes and lives, with the devastation continuing to affect those displaced by the fires.You use AI every day.
